.engramdb/memories/rounding-of-the-platform-fee-on-payouts_01a10c32-2369-7233-9921-72ddbad33cdc.md:15:The platform fee is `gross_minor * rate_bps / 10_000`, rounded up to the next minor unit with `decimal.ROUND_CEILING`, so the platform never under-collects (seller agreement, clause 7.2). The fee is at least 30 minor units per payout.
.engramdb/memories/rounding-in-proration_01a10c32-1be2-7b70-b8d5-58808404eb1f.md:15:Proration keeps full Decimal precision for the unused fraction and rounds only the final amount, to the cent, with `decimal.ROUND_HALF_DOWN`: an exact half cent stays with Acme, because the customer is already receiving a credit (Billing Ops decision BOPS-41). Never round the daily or per-second rate on its own.

.engramdb/memories/tax-uses-round-half-even_01a10c31-1855-7eb1-8cb6-551f60f7368b.md:15:Tax amounts are rounded with banker's rounding (`decimal.ROUND_HALF_EVEN`), as decided with the finance team in March 2026. Do not use ROUND_HALF_UP.
.engramdb/memories/rounding-of-percentage-refunds_01a10c32-3169-7a03-ada1-b7a7f33f7a4b.md:15:A refund given as a percentage of an invoice (goodwill refunds from support) is rounded away from zero with `decimal.ROUND_UP`, in the customer's favour. Full and fixed-amount refunds are never rounded.

Thanks. That rule is already in the project's shared memory: decision `01a10c32-0edf…` says currency conversion rounds to the target currency's smallest unit (e.g. cents) with `decimal.ROUND_FLOOR`. It's a Treasury decision from April 2026, and it's deliberately different from the rounding used for tax. What you said matches it, so I haven't added a duplicate.

I checked the code. Nothing converts currencies yet, so nothing currently breaks the rule. The only rounding in `src/` is `prorated_tax` at `src/subscriptions/proration.py:12`, which uses `ROUND_HALF_EVEN`. That's correct, because tax uses that kind of rounding by design.

When I write conversion code, I'll round down toward negative infinity. One thing to keep in mind: for negative amounts like refunds or reversals, that makes the number larger in size (−1.234 becomes −1.24). Tell me if you'd rather round toward zero in those cases.
